entries.modern_form: PIE *h₂enk- / *h₂eng- 'to bend, curve' (Pokorny '2. ank-, ang- „biegen“', IEW 45–47; Watkins/AHD 'ank-, also ang-. To bend')
entries.note: Root, language label and gloss are all correct and standard. Nourai's three-way root name 'Ang, Ank, Anq' is taken verbatim from Klein, who ends his 'angle (corner)' article (KLN p.75) with 'All these words derive fr. I.-E. base *ang-, resp. *anq-, “to bend”'. Pokorny's article runs IEW 45–47: the headword '2. ank-, ang- „biegen“; Nominalstämme anko-, onko-; ankes-; anku-lo-; anken-, -on-; ankoto-; ankro-' stands on p.45 (so Watkins cites '[Pok. 2. ank-, ang- 45]'), the sub-article 'ang-, bes. zur Bezeichnung von Gliedmaßen' with ai. áṅgam / aṅguṣṭha- = av. aṅgušta- and lat. angulus stands on p.46–47 — so POK:46 is a fair citation for the branches Nourai draws from it. Caveat for modern practice: laryngeal-era scholarship splits Pokorny's single lemma. Wiktionary keeps *h₂enk- 'curve, bend' (Skt. áñcati, Gk. ἄγκυρα, ἀγκὼν, Lat. ancus) apart from the 'limb/finger' family *h₂eng- (Skt. áṅga-, aṅguṣṭha-, Av. aṅgušta-, MP angust), and Mann (IEC) lists ang-, anghulos, anguos, ankotos, ankuros as separate lemmata, deriving Lat. angulus from *anghulos rather than *ank-. Nourai's single root box therefore merges two (probably but not certainly related) roots — the traditional Pokorny/Klein/Watkins position. Two whole limbs of the chart are, additionally, cultural loans rather than inherited descent (Gk. ἄγκυρα → Pers. langar; Skt. caturaṅga → Pahl. čatrang), which the chart's arrows do not distinguish; and the French→Persian limb (#20–#21) is wrong, see those nodes.

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt (Pokorny IEW Band I) — page marker '45' precedes '2. ank-, ang- ,biegen‘; Nominalstämme anko-, onko-; ankes-; anku-lo-; anken-, -on-; ankoto-; ankro-', and between markers '4G'(=46) and '47' stands the sub-article 'ang-, bes. zur Bezeichnung von Gliedmaßen (vgl. got. lipus ‚Glied‘: *lei- ‚biegen‘): Ai. áṅgam ‚Glied‘, aṅgūli-ḥ, aṅgūri-ḥ f. ‚Finger, Zehe‘ ... aṅguṣṭha-ḥ ‚große Zehe, Daumen‘ == av. aṅgušta- m. ‚Zehe‘' plus 'lat. angulus ... ‚Winkel‘' — exactly the material Nourai hangs on this page. Reference: WP. I 60f., WH. I 46, 49f.

consulted.note: the whole page-56 chart is essentially an English redrawing of this one Pokorny article: 'Ai. ancati (mpers. ancītan) ... ‚biegt, krümmt‘ ... av. anku-pəsəmna- ‚mit Haken, Spangen sich schmückend‘ ... av. aka- m. ‚Haken, Zapfen‘ ... ἄγκυρα ‚Anker‘ ... lat. angulus ... Much stellt hierher den lat.-germ. VN Anglii, ags. Angel, Ongel'.

'ank-. Also ang-. To bend. I. Germanic *ank- ... ANKLE. II. Suffixed form *ank-ulo-. 1. Germanic *ang-ul- in: a. Old English angul, angel, fishhook: ANGLE; b. probably Latin Angli, the Angles: ANGLE. ... III. Greek ankura, anchor: ANCHOR. ... V. Sanskrit anka, hook, ancati, he bends: PALANQUIN. ... VII. Suffixed form *ang-olo- in Latin angulus, angle, corner: ANGLE. [Pok. 2. ank-, ang- 45.]' — covers seven of Nourai's eleven root-level branches.

'L. angulus ... cogn. with Arm. angiun, ankiun, OSlav. ǫg(u)lu “corner”, OSlav. ǫkotu “hook”, Lith. anka “loop”, OI. angam “limb”, angulih, angurih “finger, toe”, angusthah “big toe, thumb”, Avestic angushta- “toe, finger”, OI. ankah “hook; bent”, ancati “bends, curves”, Gk. ἄγκος ... ἄγκυρα “anchor”, L. ancus ... All these words derive fr. I.-E. base *ang-, resp. *anq-, “to bend”' — the direct source of Nourai's root name.

one Persian headword collects AVESTAN ANGUSHTA, OLD PERSIAN ANGST, PAHLAVI ANGUST, SANSKRIT ANGAM / ANGULI / ANGA / ANKA, ARMENIAN ANGIUN, ANKIUN, GREEK ANKOS, AGKOS, ANKULUS, OLD ENGLISH ONELEOW, ENGLISH ANKLE, DANISH/SWEDISH/NORWEGIAN ANKEL, DUTCH ENKEL, LITHUANIAN — an independent modern Persian handbook grouping the family exactly as Nourai does.

nodes.derivation: Avestan aṅgušta- m. 'toe' (Bartholomae AiW 106; the sense 'finger' only in compounds, Buck 4.34) is the exact match of Sanskrit aṅguṣṭha-ḥ 'thumb, big toe' — Indo-Iranian *Hanguštʰa- built on the 'limb' base *h₂eng-u- (Skt. aṅgúli- 'finger', áṅga- 'limb') with the -stʰ(a)- formant; Indo-Iranian *-stʰ- gives Av. -št- after u. Pokorny prints the equation 'ai. aṅguṣṭha-ḥ ‚große Zehe, Daumen‘ == av. aṅgušta- m. ‚Zehe‘' (IEW 46), which is the arrow Nourai draws from the root. The word is the everyday Iranian word for 'toe/finger' and is the ancestor of every form in nodes #2 and #3.

nodes.derivation: Old Iranian *angušta- (= Av. aṅgušta-) > Middle Persian angust [ʾNGWST'] 'finger, toe; a unit of length (¾ in.)' (MacKenzie PHD 10) > New Persian angušt / angošt انگشت. Nyberg notes the dialect detail: 'angust ... SW form with -st < -št; NP angušt NW form. Paz. both angust and angušt' — i.e. the standard NP -št is the North-Western (Parthian-type) treatment, the Book-Pahlavi -st the South-Western one, so NP angošt continues the Old Iranian cluster directly rather than the SW Middle Persian output. The derivatives on the chart are transparent NP formations: انگشتر angoštar 'finger-ring' (MP angustarīg, PHD 10), انگ ۱ ang 'mark/stamp made with the finger', انگلک / انگولک angolak 'poking with a finger'. Strictly, the arrow should hang NP angošt on Middle Persian, not directly on Avestan (Avestan is a sister, not the mother, of Persian).

nodes.derivation: Sogdian ʾng(w)št / ʾnkwšt(h) 'finger' — written ʾṅgwšt in the Manichaean script and ʾnkwšt(h) in the Sogdian ('Buddhist') script, both /angušt/ — continues the same Old Iranian *angušta- as Persian angošt; Gharib's dictionary explicitly derives it from the Avestan word. The plural ʾnkwštyt and the compound pʾdʹy ʾngwšt 'toe' (lit. 'foot-finger') are attested in the Buddhist Sogdian Padmacintāmaṇi and Vimalakīrti texts.

nodes.derivation: Two Avestan words, one secure and one not. (a) aka- m. 'hook, peg' (AiW 359, also in aḵnah- 'rein') and anku- in the hapax anku-pəsəmna- 'adorning oneself with hooks/clasps' are the direct Iranian reflexes of *h₂enk-u- (= Gk. ἀγκὼν, Skt. aṅká-ḥ 'hook'); Pokorny prints both on IEW 45. That part is confirmed. (b) duždka- m. is attested only at Vidēvdād 13.2, where it is the abusive name that 'men of evil speech' (dužvacaŋhō) give the hedgehog (vaŋhāpara-, Bd. gloss xārpušt). Bartholomae's analysis *duž- 'bad' + aka- 'hook' = 'the one that has nasty hooks (spines)' is offered with an explicit '?' after 'Et.?', i.e. as a guess — which is exactly what Nourai's own NOTE says. Two further caveats: the animal is the HEDGEHOG (Igel), not the porcupine; and the first element duž- is the well-known Iranian pejorative prefix (☆ Dus), so if the etymology is right the word is a compound of two roots, only the second of which belongs on this chart.

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt, between the page markers '45' and '4G'(=46): 'av. anku-pəsəmna- ‚mit Haken, Spangen sich schmückend‘ ... av. aka- m. ‚Haken, Zapfen‘, aḵnah- (Bartholomae Stud. 2, 101, Airan. Wb. 359) ‚Zügel‘'. Both of Nourai's Avestan 'hook' words, on the cited page.

(gemeiner oder Spott)Name des sūis vaŋhāparə (‚Igel‘): spānəm .. yim vaŋhāparəm yim mašyāka avi dužvacaŋhō duzakəm nama aojaitī V.13.2. ... KompA. — Et.? Vgl. HORN KZ.34.437, HBM.AGr. ... VII. *duž+aka- ‚der schlimme Haken (Stacheln) hat‘? — mp. (Pü.): žūžak; np. žūža; Assimilation der silbenanl. Kons.' So Bartholomae has exactly Nourai's derivation but flags it 'Et.?' and appends '?' — partial support, and Nourai's NOTE correctly records the doubt. Bartholomae's gloss is 'Igel' = hedgehog, not porcupine.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian zūzag / žūžag [zwzkʹ] 'hedgehog', from Avestan duždka- by assimilation of the two syllable-initial consonants: *dužaka- > *žužag (d…ž > ž…ž), which Bartholomae states in so many words ('Assimilation der silbenanl. Kons.'). MacKenzie normalises the Book Pahlavi spelling zwzkʹ as zūzag; Bartholomae and Horn read the Pahlavi translation's form as žūžak. Nourai's third variant 'jujag' reflects the Gilaki/dialect form (Horn cites g. jūjīk) and the ambiguity of Pahlavi <z> for /ž/. The gloss should be 'hedgehog'; 'porcupine' is a loose rendering of NP خارپشت.

nodes.derivation: Sogdian ʾksyc / ʾxšyc 'hook' (Manichaean and Christian Sogdian, Henning, Sogdica 30.11a), read by Gharib as akaseč; Gharib derives it directly from Avestan aka- 'hook', i.e. from Nourai's node #4 rather than straight from the root as the chart draws it. Formally it is *aka- plus the diminutive/adjectival suffix -č (Sogd. -c), with the usual Sogdian -k- ~ -x- fluctuation before s. One caveat on the reading: the final letter is Sogdian <c>, not <e> — Nourai's 'ʿkšye' should be ʾkšyc/ʾksyc.

nodes.derivation: Ancient Greek ἄγκῦρα (ánkūra) f. 'anchor', from *h₂enk- 'bend' with the -ūra suffix, beside ἀγκὼν 'elbow, bend', ἀγκύλος 'crooked', ἄγκιστρον 'fish-hook' — the anchor named from its hooks/flukes. Attested from Homeric times onward; the place-name Ἄγκυρα (Ancyra, mod. Ankara) is the same word. Nourai's transliteration 'ankura' is a bare Latinisation of the Greek nominative.

ref_check.note: Watkins s.v. ank-: 'III. Greek ankura, anchor: ANCHOR. ... [Pok. 2. ank-, ang- 45.]' — the exact form, gloss and root Nourai gives.

nodes.derivation: A Mediterranean culture-word, not an inherited Iranian form: Gk. ἄγκυρα > Lat. ancora, whence Aramaic/Mandaic angarā and thence Middle/New Persian لنگر langar. The l- is the usual Aramaic-mediated treatment of the initial vowel + nasal (cf. the same l-/n- alternation in the Arabic reflex), and the Persian word was in turn Arabicised as أنجر ʾanjar and re-exported to Ottoman Turkish lenger, Uzbek/Turkmen langar, Gujarati, Kazakh, and Mandarin 蘭干. Mo'in's own footnote to the Borhan entry states the borrowing outright. The chart's single arrow Greek → Persian is therefore right in substance but skips the Latin/Aramaic relay. A minority view on Wiktionary keeps an alternative 'of Iranian origin, cognate with Sanskrit लङ्गल (laṅgala)', but Taqizadeh, Mo'in and Asbaghi all take the Greek/Latin route.

nodes.derivation: Sanskrit áṅga- n. 'limb, member, part of the body' (< *h₂eng-, the 'limb' branch of Pokorny's ank-/ang-), and the bahuvrīhi catur-aṅga- 'having four limbs/members' (catúr 'four', ☆ Kwetwer). In its original military sense caturaṅga- names the four arms of the Indian army — elephants, chariots, cavalry and infantry (Rigveda 10.92.11 already has catúraṅga-) — and it is from that army metaphor that the 6th-c. board game takes its name, its four pieces being precisely elephant (→ bishop), chariot/rook (→ castle), horse (→ knight) and foot-soldier (→ pawn). Nourai's gloss 'the four parts (castle, Knight, Bishop and Pawn)' therefore names the chess pieces rather than the literal 'four limbs' — the same shortcut Mo'in takes in his Borhan footnote ('شامل چهار جزء: فیل، رخ، اسب، پیاده').

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian čatrang [cʾtʾlʾng], borrowed from Sanskrit caturaṅga- with loss of the unstressed medial -u- (*čaturaṅg > čatrang) and the regular Iranian rendering of Indic -aṅga as -ang; Indic c- = MP č-. It is the title-word of the Pahlavi tract Wīzārišn ī čatrang ud nihišn ī nēw-ardaхšīr ('The Explanation of Chess and the Invention of Backgammon'), which stages the game's arrival from India at Khosrow I's court — the story Borhan-e Qate' repeats. MacKenzie lemmatises it and already flags the Arabic outcome.

nodes.derivation: The word itself and the chain are certain: MP čatrang > Classical NP چترنگ čatrang / شترنگ šatrang 'chess', Arabicised as شطرنج šaṭranj (Arabic has no /č/, so چ is rendered ش, and the t is written ط by attraction to the emphatic environment), and then re-borrowed into New Persian in that Arabic dress — a Persian→Arabic→Persian round trip. Asadi's Loġat-e Fors p.289 already has Nourai's shahid verse ('تا جز از بیست و چهارش نبود خانهٔ نرد / همچو در سی و دو خانه است نهادش شترنگ'), which Borhan quotes on the very page Nourai cites. What is suspect is the first of the two variants printed in the box, «کترنگ»: *katrang is not a Persian word, and ک vs چ differ only by the three dots — the book must be printing (or the scan misreading) چترنگ čatrang, the direct continuation of the Pahlavi form in node #12 and the form given by Mo'in, MacKenzie and Asbaghi. The second variant شطرنج is correct.

nodes.derivation: Skt. áñcati / (zero-grade) ácati 'bends, curves' is the primary verb of *h₂enk- (Pokorny prints 'Ai. ancati (mpers. ancītan) und (tiefstufig) acati ‚biegt, krümmt‘' on IEW 45), with aṅká-ḥ 'bend, hook, the hollow between chest and hip, lap' beside it. Compounded with pári 'around' (☆ Per 1) it gives pary-aṅka- ~ paly-aṅka- m. 'couch, bed, litter' — literally 'that which bends/curves around (the body)'; the ry ~ ly variation is the familiar Indic r/l fluctuation, and it is the l-form that all the borrowed words descend from (Pali pallaṅko, Prakrit pallaṅka). Nourai's gloss 'a bed carried on poles on the shoulder of two or four men … due to the sagging cloth bottom' is his own rationalisation of the palanquin sense; the standard analysis is 'bending around'.

'The basis of all the forms is Skt. paryanka, or palyanka, “a bed”, from which we have Hind. and Mahr. palang “a bed”, Hind. pālkī “a palankin”, ... Pali pallanko “a couch, bed, litter, or palankin”, and in Javanese and Malay palangki “a litter or sedan”.'

nodes.derivation: The two ends of the chain are right but the chart's single Sanskrit→English arrow leaves out the actual carriers. Skt. paly-aṅka- > Pali pallaṅko / Prakrit pallaṅka > Javanese and Malay palangki 'litter, sedan' (the Indian Ocean trade term) > Portuguese palanquim (early 16c.; the nasal -m is a standard Portuguese addition, as in mandarim, Bagaim) > English palanquin, first attested in the 1580s. The Anglo-Indian by-form palankeen/palankee comes instead from the Hindi pālkī (< Prakrit pallaṅkī), the light litter itself. Verdict 'plausible' rather than 'confirmed' only because Nourai's arrow suppresses the Prakrit–Malay–Portuguese relay that every source insists on.

nodes.derivation: Latin angulus m. 'corner, angle' (Ernout–Meillet: 'coin [d'un édifice], angle (γωνία). Ancien, technique, usuel'), from *ang-olo-, a diminutive-looking -lo- derivative of the same 'bend' base; exact cognates OCS ǫg˕l˕ 'corner' and Armenian angiwn/ankiwn 'corner', with the o-grade beside it in Lat. uncus 'hook'. Derivatives angulāris, angulātus, and the numeral compounds tri-, quadri-, rect-angulus that give English triangle and rectangle. (Mann, alone, sets it up as *anghulos with a voiced aspirate, so the exact root shape is not universally agreed.)

nodes.derivation: All three are learned Latin-via-French borrowings, not native words: L. angulus > Old French/French angle > Middle English angle (14c.) 'corner, angle'; L. tri-angulum > OF triangle > ME triangle; Late L. rect-angulum ('right-angled figure') > F rectangle > E rectangle (16c.). Klein and Skeat both label the English word '(F.–L.)'. Note that the homonym angle 'fish-hook, to fish' is NOT from Latin but the inherited Old English angel (same root, native line) — Nourai rightly keeps it off this branch, though it is the very word that node #18 depends on.

nodes.derivation: Angul (Old English Angel, Ongel; modern German Angeln, Danish Angel) is the small district on the east coast of the Jutland/Schleswig peninsula between the Schlei and Flensburg fjords, from which the Angles are said to have come. The traditional etymology, going back to Rudolf Much, identifies the name with Gmc *angul- 'fish-hook, angle' (OE angel, ON ǫngull, OHG angul) < *h₂enk-ulo-, i.e. 'the hook-shaped land' — which is exactly Nourai's gloss. It is a good but not a proven etymology: Pokorny reports it as Much's suggestion and objects that it requires 'eine sonst nicht belegte Bed. ‚Winkel; Bucht‘', and Watkins hedges with 'probably'. The language label 'Germanic' is also loose — the name is attested in Latin (Anglii, Tacitus Germania 40) and Old English/Old Norse, not in a reconstructed Proto-Germanic source.

nodes.derivation: Old English Engle / Angle (nom. pl.) 'the Angles', Latin Anglī, the Germanic people who, with the Saxons and Jutes, crossed to Britain in the mid-5th century (Bede's traditional date for the adventus Saxonum is 449; Nourai's 'around 450 AD' is the standard rounding). The i-umlaut of a > e before the following i/j of the tribal stem gives Engle beside Angle. From it: Engla land (gen. pl. 'land of the Angles') > England, and Englisc > English; the word first denoted the people, only in late Old English the country — Canute was the first king to style himself 'King of England'. Nourai's parenthesis 'Engle-Land' should be Engla land.

nodes.derivation: There is no French form 'angle-' meaning 'English' and no French link in this chain. French for 'English' is anglais, from Middle/Old French anglois, from Latin Anglus / Late Latin Anglenses — i.e. from the LATIN form of the tribal name (Tacitus's Anglii, Bede's Angli), not from Old English Engle as the chart's arrow claims; Latin took the name from Germanic independently of Old English. The French word angle is a different lexeme altogether: 'corner', from Latin angulus, which is Nourai's own node #16. The node therefore conflates two homographs and inserts an intermediary that no source supports; and its child, Persian انگلیس, is not derived from French anyway (see #21).

nodes.derivation: Persian انگلیس is a modern European loan, but the accepted source is Italian inglese, most probably relayed through Ottoman Turkish انگلیز ingiliz — the Levantine-trade route by which most early-modern European ethnonyms reached Persian — not the French route Nourai draws (and certainly not from any French 'angle-'). The final -s of انگلیس matches Italian -se, not French -ais /ɛ/; انگلیسی englisi is the ordinary Persian nisba of it, and انگلستان englestān is an internal Persian -stān formation ('land of the English'), not a borrowing at all. The ultimate origin in Latin Anglus < the Germanic tribal name is of course correct; it is the immediate donor language that is wrong.
